unit.unitTitle: Reading a Whole Sentence: Ready for Intro

cefr.bandName: Pre-A1, before any English at all

unit.unitOverview:
No new spellings. You have them all.
Six words that break every rule.
Then a whole sentence, left to right.
Then the Intro level.
unit.learningPath:
Listen to the lesson.
Words: six hard ones, and the words for reading.
Patterns: the hard words, sentences, going on.
Read three short texts.
Read a sentence out loud. Record it.
Write sentences of your own.
Practice and quiz. Check your answers.
functions: Read the words that phonics cannot read
Find where a sentence starts and ends
Read a whole sentence from left to right
Read a sentence out loud, without stopping
Write a sentence with a capital and a full stop
Say what you can do now and what comes next

visual.lectureScript:
This is Unit 20. The last one.
There are no new spellings today.
You have every one of them.
Two things left. Then you are done.
The first is a short list of words.
These break every rule you have learned.
You cannot sound them out. Nobody can.
Would. Could. Two. Four. Because. People.
Look at would. W, o, u, l, d.
The l says nothing at all.
Look at two. T, w, o.
The w says nothing either.
People. That should be pee-oh-ple.
It is not. It is pee-pl.
There are about a hundred words like this.
A hundred, out of many thousands.
You learn them by sight, the way you did the.
And you meet them every single day.
So they come quickly.
Now the second thing. A whole sentence.
Until now you read words. One at a time.
A sentence is words in a line, with a job.
It starts with a capital letter.
It ends with a full stop.
Those two marks tell you where to start.
And where to stop and take a breath.
Read left to right. Always left to right.
Do not look ahead. Do not jump back.
If a word stops you, say its sounds.
Then go on. Do not start the line again.
Read the whole sentence. Then read it once more.
The second time is always better.
That is the last thing this level teaches.
And now you are ready for the Intro level.
Intro does not teach reading. It teaches English.
Your name. Your job. The time. A shop.
It asks you to read, and now you can.
Twenty units. Well done. Go on.

readings.title: The First Day
readings.genre: Whole sentences, with capitals and full stops
readings.setting: A first morning at a new job
readings.passageScript:
I would not say it was fun.
Two people came with me.
We were late because the bus did not stop.
The man at the gate had four names on a list.
He said: you are late, but go in.
I could read the list.
That was new, and it felt good.

grammar.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
grammar.title: The words phonics cannot read
grammar.explanation:
Some words break every rule.
You cannot work them out. Nobody can.
There are about a hundred, and you meet them daily.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
would   the l says nothing
could   the l says nothing
two     the w says nothing
four    not like for
because not like cause
people  said pee-pl
grammar.workedExample:
You meet the word people.
1. Try the sounds first. Always.
2. Pee-oh-ple. That is not a word.
3. So it is one of the hundred.
4. Look at it. Say it. Look away. Say it.
5. Three times a day for three days.
grammar.commonMistake:
Grinding at a word that cannot be decoded.
Try the sounds once. If it fails, learn it whole.
grammar.memoryTip: A hundred words. Thousands follow the rules.
grammar.practice:
Read these by sight.
1. would
2. could
3. two
4. four
5. because
6. people
grammar.answerKey:
There is no working out here.
Check: each one read without stopping?
Not yet? Look, say, look away, say.

grammar.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
grammar.title: Where a sentence starts and ends
grammar.explanation:
A sentence is words in a line, saying one thing.
Two marks tell you where it begins and ends.
Find them before you read.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
The bus was late.
^                ^
capital          full stop

A capital letter starts it.
A full stop ends it.
That is where you breathe.
grammar.workedExample:
You see a long line of words.
1. Find the first capital letter.
2. That is where the sentence starts.
3. Now look for the next full stop.
4. That is where it ends.
5. Read from one to the other. Then breathe.
grammar.commonMistake:
Reading past a full stop runs two ideas together.
Stop at the dot. Take a breath.
grammar.memoryTip: Capital to full stop. Then breathe.
grammar.practice:
How many sentences? Count the full stops.
1. I got up. I went to work.
2. The bus was late.
3. It was cold. I had no coat. I ran.
4. She said no.
5. We ate. Then we went home.
6. Well done.
grammar.answerKey:
1. two
2. one
3. three
4. one
5. two
6. one
Five or six right? You can see a sentence.

grammar.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
grammar.title: Reading a whole sentence
grammar.explanation:
Until now you read one word at a time.
Now you read a line of them, in order.
Left to right. Never back.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
1. Start at the capital.
2. Read each word, left to right.
3. A word stops you? Say its sounds.
4. Then go ON. Do not start again.
5. Stop at the full stop.
6. Now read the whole thing once more.
grammar.workedExample:
You read: The people were late because of the bus.
1. Capital T. Start there.
2. The. People. Were. Late.
3. Because stops you. Say it by sight.
4. Go on. Of. The. Bus.
5. Full stop. Breathe. Read it again.
grammar.commonMistake:
Going back to the start after every hard word.
You never reach the end that way. Go on.
grammar.memoryTip: One hard word does not cost the sentence.
grammar.practice:
Read each sentence twice. Was the second better?
1. I would like a cup of tea.
2. Two people were late.
3. I could not read it because it was dark.
4. Four of us went home.
grammar.answerKey:
There is no written key.
Check: did you read left to right each time?
Did you go on after a hard word?
Was the second reading better than the first?

grammar.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
grammar.title: What the Intro level asks of you
grammar.explanation:
This level taught you to read the letters.
The next one teaches English.
It asks you to read, and now you can.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Phonics    the sounds, the spellings, the words
Intro      your name, your job, the time, a shop

Intro has 16 units.
It reads at about the level you are now.
It will not ask you to sound out a word.
grammar.workedExample:
You are about to start Intro.
1. You can read a short sentence.
2. You can sound out a word you do not know.
3. You know the hundred hard words are hard.
4. That is everything Intro needs.
5. Keep a word list. Read it out loud daily.
grammar.commonMistake:
Stopping here because it feels unfinished.
Reading gets better by being used, not by more phonics.
grammar.memoryTip: Read every day. Ten minutes beats an hour.
grammar.practice:
Say these out loud, about yourself.
1. I can read a sentence.
2. I am ready for the next level.
3. The next level is Intro.
4. Well done.
grammar.answerKey:
There is no key. These are yours to say.
Check: did you say all four out loud?
Did you mean them? You should.

assignments.title: Read a sentence, and write four
assignments.instructions:
Two parts.
1. Record yourself. Read the six hard words.
would, could, two, four, because, people
Then read these two sentences, twice each:
I could not read it because it was dark.
Two people were late for work today.
2. Write four sentences about your day.
A capital at the start. A full stop at the end.
Use because in one of them.
Listen back before you finish.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
teacherNotes.note: Every pattern card has a worked example, every practice has a key, and every speaking task ends with record, listen back, check.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
teacherNotes.noteType: The hard words come last for a reason
teacherNotes.note: would, could, two, four, because and people are among the commonest words in English and none of them can be decoded. Meeting them in Unit 2 would have taught a beginner that phonics does not work. Meeting them now, after two hundred decoded words, teaches that English has a short list of exceptions. Say the number: about a hundred, out of many thousands.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
teacherNotes.noteType: Going on after a hard word is the whole skill
teacherNotes.note: The commonest failure at this point is not misreading a word; it is going back to the start of the line after every one. The learner then reads the first four words ten times and never reaches the end. Say it plainly and watch for it. One hard word does not cost the sentence.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
teacherNotes.noteType: The second reading is where fluency comes from
teacherNotes.note: Re-reading the same sentence is not a remedial move, it is the move. 1SLp.01 is exactly this: re-read sentences aloud with some fluency. A learner who reads everything once and moves on stays slow for years.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
teacherNotes.noteType: Do not hold a learner here
teacherNotes.note: Reading improves by being used, not by more phonics. A learner who can decode a short sentence and knows the hard words are hard has everything Intro needs. If they feel unfinished, that is normal and is not a reason to repeat units — Intro reads at about this level and never asks them to sound out a word.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
teacherNotes.noteType: Say well done, and say what changed
teacherNotes.note: Twenty units is a great deal of work for an adult who could not read at the start. The word list in this unit is the evidence: four words in Unit 2, over two hundred now. Put the two numbers side by side out loud. It is the most motivating thing in the level and it costs ten seconds.
